key_terms.meaning: Implanted or external device that gives a small timed current pulse to start a heartbeat when natural conduction fails.
Device that gives one large controlled shock to stop chaotic fibrillation so a normal rhythm can restart.
Cardiopulmonary bypass circuit that pumps blood and oxygenates it while the heart is stopped.
A named combination of how each breath is triggered, limited and cycled (ended), such as volume control, pressure control, pressure support or SIMV.
Device that adds water vapour to dry medical gas before it reaches the airway.
Device that turns liquid medicine or water into fine droplets for inhalation.
Deep heating by radio-frequency current, commonly 27.12 MHz, passed through tissue without cutting skin.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation; low-amplitude pulses through skin used mainly to relieve pain.
Neuromuscular electrical stimulation; current pulses that make a muscle contract for training or function.
Electrical muscle stimulation; use of current pulses to produce muscle contraction.
Functional electrical stimulation; NMES timed to help a useful movement such as grasping or walking.
Two medium-frequency currents crossed in tissue; their difference frequency stimulates nerve.
Time for which each current pulse is on, usually measured in microseconds or milliseconds.
Number of pulses or cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Strength of a current or voltage pulse, measured in milliamperes (mA) or volts (V).
Q = I × t, where I is current in amperes and t is pulse width in seconds; measured in coulombs (C).
Breaking a kidney stone with focused shock waves so small pieces pass out in urine.
Cold probe cooled by liquid nitrogen or expanding gas that freezes and destroys tissue.
Circuit that limits the high shock voltage reaching an ECG amplifier during defibrillation.
Catheter that delivers radio-frequency energy to destroy a small patch of heart muscle causing an arrhythmia.

takeaways: A pacemaker gives a small timed pulse to start a beat; a defibrillator gives one large shock to stop fibrillation.
A heart-lung machine replaces both the heart's pumping and the lung's gas exchange during open-heart surgery.
Every ventilator breath is triggered, limited and cycled; the cycle variable (volume, pressure, time, flow or the patient) ends inspiration, and a mode combines these choices.
Dry medical gas injures the airway, so water is added as vapour, droplets or a measured inhaled drug dose.
Diathermy heats deep tissue with radio-frequency current, microwaves or ultrasound without cutting the skin.
Electrical stimulation uses controlled current pulses to relieve pain, retrain muscle or find a nerve.
Lithotripsy breaks stones with focused shock waves, and cryotherapy destroys lesions with deep cold.
Protection circuits and careful catheter energy delivery keep therapeutic shocks from damaging the patient or the monitor.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for block diagrams, waveforms, electrode or catheter placement, mode selection, safety hazards, and internal-versus-external comparisons.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of an implantable cardiac pacemaker and explain each block, including the pulse generator, battery, leads and timing control.
outline: Block diagram with battery, oscillator/timing, output pulse circuit, lead and electrodes
Why the pulse is small and timed
answer: Purpose. When the sinus node fails or the AV conduction is blocked, the heart beats too slowly. The pacemaker supplies the missing trigger: a small, timed pulse at the tip of a lead in the right ventricle depolarises the muscle around it, and the muscle then contracts and pumps by itself.

svg.aria: Block diagram of a demand pacemaker: lithium-iodine cell, timing oscillator, output circuit, coupling capacitor, lead and tip electrode, heart, and a sense amplifier whose output resets the timer.

answer: Battery. A lithium-iodine cell gives about 2.8 V and 1–2.5 Ah. Its self-discharge is very low and its voltage falls slowly and predictably near the end, so the unit can signal "replacement due" months ahead.

Timing circuit. A crystal or RC oscillator sets the escape interval. At 70 ppm the interval is 60 ÷ 70 = 0.857 s, so a pulse is due 857 ms after the last beat. After each pulse or sensed beat there is a refractory period of about 250–300 ms in which the sense input is ignored, so the T wave and the pacemaker's own pulse are not counted as beats.

Output circuit. Between beats a small output capacitor charges from the cell; at the end of the interval a switch empties it into the lead. Each pulse is a rectangle of about 2.5–5 V lasting about 0.5 ms. The coupling capacitor passes the pulse but blocks any steady current, which would corrode the electrode and injure the tissue.

Lead and electrodes. The lead is a coiled, silicone- or polyurethane-insulated wire passed through the subclavian or cephalic vein to the right ventricular apex, held by tines or a screw. In a unipolar lead the current runs from the tip to the metal case; in a bipolar lead it runs between the tip and a ring 1–2 cm behind it, so the sensed signal picks up less muscle noise.

Sense amplifier. It picks up the R wave inside the heart, about 5–20 mV, through a band-pass filter that rejects the slow T wave and fast muscle noise. A sensed beat resets the timer, so no pulse is sent: this is demand pacing.

head: Fixed rate (VOO)
Demand (VVI)
rows: still fires: competition, risk of a pulse on the T wave
magnet test mode, surgery with diathermy

answer.text: Why the pulse is small and timed. The stimulus only has to exceed the capture threshold, usually below 1 V, with a safety margin of two to three times. With 2.5 V into 500 Ω for 0.5 ms at 70 ppm and a 10 µA circuit drain:
answer.pre:
I = 2.5 / 500 = 5 mA;  q = 5 mA × 0.5 ms = 2.5 µC per pulse
pacing current = 2.5 µC × 70/60 = 2.92 µA
I<sub>avg</sub> = 2.92 + 10 = 12.92 µA → 12.92 µA × 8760 h = 0.1132 Ah per year
life = 1.2 Ah / 0.1132 = 10.6 years

answer: A wider or bigger pulse would capture no better but would shorten that life. The pulse energy is only 2.5 V × 5 mA × 0.5 ms = 6.25 µJ.

Battery and lead safety. The titanium case is welded shut and the feedthroughs are sealed so body fluid cannot enter. Zener diodes across the output protect the circuit from defibrillator and electrosurgery currents. A magnet over the case closes a reed switch and gives fixed-rate pacing for testing. Lead fracture, insulation break, dislodgement and pocket infection are the main lead hazards; strong fields from MRI and diathermy can inhibit or damage the unit.
Closing check: 857 ms × 70 = 60 s; 2.5 µC × 70/60 = 2.92 µA; 1.2 Ah / (12.92 µA × 8760 h) = 10.6 years, inside the real 7–12 years.

bank.q: Explain the principle and block diagram of a heart-lung machine. How does it replace both the heart and the lungs during surgery?
outline: Blood pump, oxygenator, heat exchanger, reservoir and tubing circuit
Venous drainage, oxygenation, carbon dioxide removal and arterial return
Why the heart can be stopped
answer: Principle. The heart-lung machine drains venous blood out of the body, does the lung's job (adds oxygen, removes carbon dioxide) and the heart's job (pumps it at a set flow and pressure), and returns it to the aorta. Heart and lungs are bypassed, so the surgeon can stop and open the heart.

svg.aria: Block diagram of the bypass loop: venous cannula in the right atrium, venous reservoir with level sensor, pump at 4.04 litres per minute, oxygenator, heat exchanger, arterial filter with bubble detector, and aortic cannula.

head: Block
Job
Working value
rows: drains blood from the right atrium by gravity
stores blood, lets bubbles rise out, steadies the pump supply
level sensor stops the pump if low
replaces the lungs: O₂ in, CO₂ out across a thin membrane

answer.text: Setting the flow for a 170 cm, 60 kg patient:

answer: How it replaces the heart. The pump delivers that flow against the patient's vascular resistance; the perfusionist keeps the mean arterial pressure at 50–80 mmHg. A roller pump is occlusive and needs a pressure limit; a centrifugal pump is non-occlusive, so its flow must be measured with a flow probe.

How it replaces the lungs. Gas flows on one side of the membrane and blood on the other. Raising the oxygen fraction of the sweep gas raises the blood oxygen; raising the sweep gas flow washes out more CO₂. Blood gases are checked regularly. The ventilator is stopped once full flow is reached.

Why the heart can be stopped. With the full venous return taken by the circuit, the aorta is cross-clamped above the coronary arteries and a cold, potassium-rich cardioplegia solution is given through a separate line. The heart stops in diastole and is cooled, which lowers its oxygen need, so it survives the ischaemic time. After the repair the clamp is removed, the heart is restarted, and bypass is weaned while the lungs are ventilated again.

head: Hazard
Cause
Control
rows: heparin before cannulation, clotting time checked; protamine at the end
level sensor, bubble detector, arterial filter, careful priming
centrifugal pump, small circuits, haematocrit checks
battery backup and a hand crank

answer: Closing check: 1.6833 m² × 2.4 = 4.04 L/min; the circuit has a pump for the heart, an oxygenator for the lungs, and a sensor guarding each of the two killers, air and clot.

bank.q: List the variables that can end inspiration in a ventilator and explain volume-cycled, pressure-cycled, time-cycled, flow-cycled and patient-cycled modes.
outline: Definition of a breath cycle: inspiration and expiration
Volume, pressure, time, flow and patient triggering
One clinical use of each mode
answer: Breath cycle. A breath has inspiration, when gas flows into the lungs, and expiration, when it flows out passively. A ventilator controls four phase variables: the trigger starts inspiration, the limit caps a variable during it, the cycle ends it, and the baseline sets the pressure the patient exhales to (PEEP).

What cycling means. The cycle variable is the measured quantity that, on reaching its set value, switches the ventilator from inspiration to expiration: the inspiratory valve closes and the expiratory valve opens.

head: Cycle
Inspiration ends when
What can vary
Clinical use
rows: the set tidal volume has been delivered
pressure rises if the lungs stiffen
airway pressure reaches the set value
the set inspiratory time has passed
flow falls to a set fraction of its peak

answer.text: Time cycling with numbers. Rate 15 breaths/min and I:E 1:2:
answer.pre:
breath = 60 / 15 = 4 s
T<sub>i</sub> = 4 / 3 = 1.33 s;  T<sub>e</sub> = 2.67 s
with V<sub>t</sub> = 500 mL at constant flow: 0.5 L / 1.33 s = 0.375 L/s

answer: Volume cycling. The ventilator counts the volume delivered and stops at the set value, for example 500 mL. Volume is guaranteed, so a high-pressure limit is essential: if the lungs stiffen or the tube blocks, pressure rises instead.
Pressure cycling. The breath ends when the airway reaches the set pressure. A stiffer lung reaches it sooner, so the tidal volume falls without warning unless exhaled volume is monitored.

Pressure control is time-cycled. The pressure rises to its limit early in the breath; cycling on that pressure would end inspiration at once. So the limit is pressure and the cycle is time: the mode is named for its limit.

answer.text: Flow cycling. In pressure support the flow is high at first and falls as the lung fills. With a peak flow of 60 L/min and the usual 25 % setting:
answer.pre: cycle when flow = 0.25 × 60 = 15 L/min

answer: Patient cycling. In CPAP the patient breathes spontaneously at a constant raised pressure; each breath ends when the patient stops inhaling.

answer.text: Alarm and safety checks for every mode:

head: Alarm
Guards against
rows: blocked or kinked tube, coughing, stiff lung (volume modes)
Low exhaled tidal or minute volume

answer: Closing check: 60 / 15 = 4 s; 1.33 + 2.67 = 4 s; 0.375 L/s × 1.33 s = 0.5 L, the set tidal volume.

bank.q: Compare a humidifier, a nebulizer and an inhaler. Why is each used in respiratory care?
outline: Humidifier adds vapour to dry gas
Nebulizer makes fine droplets from liquid
Inhaler delivers a measured drug dose
Site of action and typical use
Hazards of over-humidification or wrong dose
answer: The common problem. Gas from a cylinder or pipeline is almost dry, while the airway needs gas at 37 °C carrying 44 mg of water per litre. Respiratory care also needs a way to put drugs into the lung. Three devices answer these needs differently.

head: Humidifier
Nebulizer
Inhaler (MDI or DPI)
rows: liquid droplets, with or without drug
jet (venturi and baffle), ultrasonic crystal, vibrating mesh
pressurised canister with valve, or powder broken up by the breath
MMAD 1–5 µm for the lower airway
about 1–5 µm; a spacer removes the big ones
whole airway: keeps mucus thin and cilia moving
oxygen therapy, ventilated or tracheostomy patients
acute asthma, children, patients who cannot coordinate an inhaler
regular asthma and COPD treatment at home
wrong technique, dose in the throat

answer.text: How much water a humidifier must add for 10 L/min of dry oxygen:

answer: Humidifier. It adds water as vapour and never carries a drug. A heated humidifier warms a chamber so the gas can hold 44 mg/L; a heated-wire circuit stops rainout. A heat-and-moisture exchanger recycles exhaled heat and water for short use.

Nebulizer. A jet nebulizer uses gas at 6–8 L/min through a venturi; liquid is drawn up and broken on a baffle. An ultrasonic nebulizer uses a piezoelectric crystal and a mesh nebulizer pushes liquid through a vibrating plate. The aim is MMAD 1–5 µm: bigger droplets stop in the mouth and throat, smaller ones are breathed out.

Inhaler. One press of a metered-dose inhaler releases a fixed dose, for example 100 µg of salbutamol; a spacer slows the cloud so less lands in the throat. A dry-powder inhaler needs a fast inspiratory flow to break up the powder.

Hazards of over-humidification and wrong dose. Too much water causes rainout that can run into the patient, wet flow sensors, blocked tubes and, in infants, water overload; a dirty reservoir spreads infection. A nebulizer or inhaler used with poor technique gives too little drug in the lung; too many inhaler puffs give tremor and a fast heart rate.
Closing check: humidifier = vapour, no drug; nebulizer = droplets, can carry a drug; inhaler = measured drug dose; 44 × 10 × 60 / 1000 = 26.4 g/h.

bank.q: A patient with ventricular fibrillation needs external defibrillation. Explain electrode placement, the shock waveform, and how the defibrillator protection circuit protects the ECG monitor.
outline: Why a large shock stops fibrillation
Protection circuit limits voltage at ECG input
answer: Why a large shock stops fibrillation. In ventricular fibrillation many small wavelets of activation circle the ventricles, so they quiver and do not pump. A shock that depolarises a critical mass of muscle at the same moment makes every cell refractory together; the wavelets have nowhere to go and die out, and the sinus node can take over.

External electrode placement. Anterolateral: one paddle or pad below the right clavicle beside the sternum, the other over the apex in the left mid-axillary line (the V6 position). Anteroposterior: one over the front of the heart, one on the back below the left scapula. Gel pads lower the chest impedance to about 50–100 Ω and prevent burns. Keep pads off the ECG electrodes and at least about 8 cm from an implanted pacemaker.

answer.text: The DC defibrillator and its energy (32 µF charged to 5000 V):
answer.pre:
E = ½ C V² = 0.5 × 32 × 10⁻⁶ × (5000)² = 400 J stored
Q = C V = 32 × 10⁻⁶ × 5000 = 0.16 C
chest 50 Ω, internal 10 Ω: 50 / 60 = 0.83 → 333 J delivered
peak current at the start = 5000 / 60 = 83 A

head: Monophasic
Biphasic
rows: damped half-sine (Lown, series inductor), current one way
works at lower energy, less muscle injury, adjusts to chest impedance

answer: Mode. For VF the shock is unsynchronised and fires at once. For atrial fibrillation or flutter it is synchronised to the R wave so it never falls on the T wave, where it could start VF.

svg.aria: Protection chain between the ECG electrodes and the amplifier: series resistors of 20 kilohms in each lead limit the current to 125 milliamperes, a neon lamp fires at 60 to 100 volts and shunts the shock, and clamp diodes hold the amplifier input to the supply rails.

answer.pre:
two 20 kΩ series resistors: 5000 V / 40 kΩ = 125 mA at most
neon lamp fires at 60–100 V and shunts the current
clamp diodes hold the input within the supply rails (a few volts)

answer: Order of action. The series resistors limit the current first, the neon lamp or spark gap then carries the shock current past the amplifier, and the diodes clamp what remains. After the shock the amplifier is saturated and the lamp is ionised, so the trace returns after a fraction of a second to a few seconds. This protects the monitor, not the patient.

Safety of operator and patient. Call "stand clear" and check that nobody touches the patient or bed; remove oxygen from the chest area to avoid fire; dry the chest; never fire paddles in the air or together; use defibrillator-proof ECG leads; check the electrode contact so the current does not burn the skin.

bank.q: Set up volume-cycled ventilation for an adult with stiff lungs. State the settings you would check, how the breath ends, and what alarms you would verify.
outline: Peak pressure and plateau pressure limits
answer: The patient. An adult man, 175 cm tall, with stiff lungs (for example acute lung injury). Stiff lungs mean low compliance: a normal volume needs a high pressure, which overstretches the alveoli, so the volume is kept small and the pressures are watched.

answer.text: Tidal volume from predicted body weight:

head: Setting
Value
Reason
rows: keeps minute ventilation up with small breaths
plateau and resistance can be measured
keeps alveoli open in stiff lungs
start at 1.0, lower to keep SpO₂ 88–95 %

answer.pre:
breath = 60 / 18 = 3.33 s;  T<sub>i</sub> = 3.33 / 3 = 1.11 s;  T<sub>e</sub> = 2.22 s
minute ventilation = 0.424 L × 18 = 7.63 L/min
inspiratory flow = 0.424 L / 1.11 s = 0.382 L/s = 22.9 L/min

answer: How the breath ends. The ventilator delivers the constant flow until 424 mL has passed its flow sensor, then the volume cycle closes the inspiratory valve and opens the expiratory valve. An inspiratory pause of about 0.5 s lets the plateau pressure be read.

answer.text: Pressure limits. Suppose the monitor shows a peak of 35 and a plateau of 28 cmH₂O:
answer.pre:
compliance = 424 mL / (28 − 10) cmH₂O = 23.6 mL/cmH₂O (stiff)
driving pressure = 28 − 10 = 18 cmH₂O
resistance = (35 − 28) / 0.382 = 18.3 cmH₂O per L/s

answer: Plateau pressure must stay below 30 cmH₂O and driving pressure is best kept below about 15 cmH₂O; here 18 cmH₂O is high, so the tidal volume would be lowered toward 4–5 mL/kg and the rate raised. The resistance is also high, so the tube is suctioned and checked for kinks.

head: Alarm
Setting
Meaning
rows: about 40 cmH₂O, near 5–10 above the peak
blocked tube, coughing, worse compliance; the breath is cut short

answer.text: Humidification need. The tube bypasses the nose, so a heated humidifier must condition the whole minute ventilation:
answer.pre: 44 mg/L × 7.63 L/min = 336 mg/min → 20.1 g of water per hour

bank.q: Choose TENS or NMES for two cases: chronic pain and weak muscle after nerve injury. Give suitable amplitude, frequency and pulse width reasoning.
outline: Frequency in Hz and pulse width in microseconds or milliseconds
answer: Both use the same pulse generator: a constant-current output whose dose is amplitude, pulse width and frequency. The difference is the target fibre. TENS excites large sensory fibres (Aβ) and no motor fibres; NMES excites motor nerves so the muscle contracts.

Case 1: chronic low-back pain. Choose TENS. By gate control, signals in the large Aβ fibres close a gate in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, so the small pain fibres (Aδ and C) cannot pass their signals up.

head: Parameter
Conventional TENS
Acupuncture-like TENS
Reasoning
rows: high rate fires Aβ fibres steadily; low rate releases endorphins
short pulses reach sensory threshold before motor threshold
below motor threshold for conventional TENS
relief lasts minutes to hours after

answer.text: Dose of conventional TENS at 20 mA, 100 µs, 100 Hz:
answer.pre:
Q = 20 mA × 100 µs = 2 µC per pulse
D = 100 µs × 100 Hz = 0.01 = 1 %
average current = 20 mA × 0.01 = 0.2 mA

answer: Case 2: weak quadriceps after a partial nerve injury. Choose NMES. The surviving motor axons are fired by the current, the muscle contracts and its strength and bulk are rebuilt.

head: Parameter
Value
Reasoning
rows: fuses twitches into a smooth (tetanic) contraction; higher rates tire the muscle
longer pulses recruit motor fibres at lower current
20–80 mA, to a visible strong contraction
set by response; constant current keeps it steady
10 s on, 30 s off, with 1–2 s ramps
rest prevents fatigue; ramps make it comfortable

answer.text: Dose of NMES at 50 mA, 300 µs, 35 Hz, 10 s on and 30 s off, 5 cm × 5 cm electrodes:
answer.pre:
Q = 50 mA × 300 µs = 15 µC per pulse;  15 µC / 25 cm² = 0.6 µC/cm²
D = 300 µs × 35 Hz = 0.0105 → 0.525 mA average while on
over a 40 s cycle: 0.525 × 10 / 40 = 0.13 mA

answer: If the nerve is completely cut, the muscle is denervated and these short pulses cannot excite it; the muscle membrane itself needs much longer pulses, tens of milliseconds, until the nerve regrows.

Electrode placement. TENS: two electrodes over or around the painful area, or along the nerve or dermatome that supplies it. NMES: one electrode on the motor point of the muscle (where the smallest current gives a contraction) and one over the muscle belly further along.

Contraindications. Not over the chest or neck of a patient with a pacemaker, not over the carotid sinus, the pregnant abdomen, broken skin, a tumour or a deep-vein thrombosis, and not on a patient who cannot report sensation.
Closing check: 20 mA × 100 µs = 2 µC; 50 mA × 300 µs = 15 µC; 15 / 25 = 0.6 µC/cm².

bank.q: Describe extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy. How are shock waves generated, focused and coupled to the stone?
outline: Focusing by ellipsoid, lens or acoustic method
answer: Principle. Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy breaks a kidney or upper-ureter stone with pressure pulses made outside the body and focused on the stone. The compressive wave enters the stone, reflects from its back face as a tensile wave that cracks it, and cavitation bubbles erode the front face. The aim is fragments of 1–2 mm that pass in the urine.

head: Source
How the pulse is made
Focusing
rows: about 80 nF at 15–25 kV discharged across a spark gap under water
current pulse in a flat coil drives a metal membrane
hundreds of ceramic crystals on a bowl fire together

answer.text: Energy of the electrohydraulic source (80 nF at 20 kV, 2500 shocks):
answer.pre:
E = ½ C V² = 0.5 × 80 × 10⁻⁹ × (20 × 10³)² = 16 J per shock
session = 16 J × 2500 = 40 kJ

answer.text: Focusing by the ellipsoid. Every point P on an ellipsoid has PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a. For a = 150 mm and b = 90 mm:
answer.pre:
c = √(150² − 90²) = √14 400 = 120 mm
F₁F₂ = 2c = 240 mm (spark to stone)
every reflected path = 2a = 300 mm → 0.300 / 1500 = 0.2 ms
all rays arrive together, so the pressure adds at F₂

answer: The spark sits at F₁, inside the reflector; the stone is brought to F₂, the far focus at a fixed distance. Peak pressure at F₂ is tens of megapascals, in a focal zone a few millimetres wide and a few centimetres long.

Water or gel coupling. Air reflects nearly all the acoustic energy because its impedance is far below that of tissue. So the path from source to skin is water: once a bath, now a water-filled cushion pressed to the flank with gel. Air bubbles in the gel are removed, or the wave is blocked and the skin bruised.

Imaging and targeting. Fluoroscopy (X-ray) or ultrasound locates the stone in two planes; the table is moved until the stone sits on the cross-hairs at F₂. Imaging is repeated during the session because breathing moves the kidney.

answer.pre:
2500 shocks at 90 per minute → 2500 / 90 = 27.8 min
start at low energy and step up
stop when the fragments look small enough

answer: Firing at 60–120 shocks per minute, rather than faster, gives the cavitation bubbles time to dissolve so they do not scatter the next shock. Electrohydraulic units may be gated to the R wave so a shock cannot fall on the T wave.
Fragments pass in urine. The patient drinks plenty of water; fragments pass over days to weeks. A ureteric stent can keep urine flowing if a column of fragments might block the ureter.

Pain control and safety. Analgesia or light sedation is enough with modern sources, especially piezoelectric ones, which spread the energy over a large skin area. Contraindications: pregnancy, bleeding disorders or anticoagulants, untreated urinary infection, obstruction below the stone, and an aneurysm near the path. Stones above about 2 cm, cystine stones and very obese patients do better with another method.
Closing check: ½ × 80 nF × (20 kV)² = 16 J; √(150² − 90²) = 120 mm; 0.3 m / 1500 m/s = 0.2 ms.

bank.q: Plan cryotherapy for a small skin lesion. Explain the cryogen, freeze-thaw cycle, probe or spray method, and safety checks.
outline: Liquid nitrogen or expanding gas cooling
answer: The lesion. A common wart 6 mm across and about 3 mm deep on the back of the hand. The goal is to bring every cell of it below −40 °C, the temperature below which almost no cell survives, while sparing the skin around it.

Cryogen. Liquid nitrogen, which boils at −196 °C, applied by spray from a hand-held flask or with a cotton swab; nitrous oxide (about −89 °C, Joule–Thomson cooling) through a closed probe is an alternative for small lesions.

Probe contact or spray. A spray is held 1–2 cm from the skin and aimed at the centre; a probe is pressed on with a little gel so it freezes on. The ice field should extend about 2 mm beyond the edge of the lesion, because the edge of the ice is near 0 °C and the lethal −40 °C line lies inside it.

answer.text: How much heat must be removed. Take the frozen volume as a cylinder 10 mm across (6 mm plus a 2 mm margin all round) and 3 mm deep, density 1 g/cm³, and 468.7 J per gram to reach −40 °C:

answer: In practice far more nitrogen is used, because most of the spray boils off in the air.

head: Step
What to do
Why
rows: spray until the white ice field reaches 2 mm beyond the edge, then hold 10–30 s
let it thaw by itself for 1–2 minutes; do not warm it
crystals grow and water floods the shrunken cells
cells weakened by the first cycle die
let it thaw again by itself

answer: How the tissue dies. Ice forms first between the cells, the remaining fluid becomes very salty and draws water out of the cells, and fast cooling also forms ice inside them. On thawing, water rushes back and bursts the weakened membranes, and the small vessels clot, so the lesion loses its blood supply.

Protect the surrounding skin. Use a plastic cone or an ear speculum held on the skin to confine the spray, or a probe the size of the lesion; keep it away from the eyes, and treat thin skin and dark skin, where loss of pigment shows, with shorter freezes.

Safety checks. Wear eye protection; carry and pour nitrogen in a vented flask, never a sealed one; store dewars in a ventilated room with an oxygen monitor; never touch the frosted nozzle with bare skin.

Wound care and follow-up. A blister forms within hours and a crust within days; keep it clean and dry and do not pick it. It heals in about 1–3 weeks. Review at 3 weeks and repeat the treatment if any wart remains.

bank.q: Compare internal and external pacemakers and defibrillators. Include batteries, AC and DC operation, electrode or lead placement, and safety.
outline: Pulse energy and shock energy difference
answer: Both machines exist in internal and external forms. Internal devices sit in or on the heart and need little energy; external devices work through the skin and chest and need much more.

head: Internal (implanted)
External
rows: generator under the collarbone; lead through a vein to the right ventricle
large pads on the chest (transcutaneous) or a temporary wire through a vein
lithium-iodine cell, 2.8 V, 1–2.5 Ah, about 7–12 years
replaceable battery, such as a 9 V cell
emergencies, after heart surgery, until an implant

answer.pre:
implanted: 2.5 V × 5 mA × 0.5 ms = 6.25 µJ
transcutaneous: I²R t = (0.07 A)² × 100 Ω × 0.04 s = 19.6 mJ, about 3000 times more

head: Internal
External
rows: paddles on the heart in open-chest surgery; ICD leads in the right ventricle
paddles or pads on the chest, anterolateral or anteroposterior
5–50 J on the heart; ICD up to about 35–40 J
120–200 J biphasic, up to 360 J monophasic
mains unit in theatre; ICD runs on its own lithium cell
mains with battery backup, or battery in an AED

answer.text: AC versus DC operation. The early AC defibrillator applied mains through a step-up transformer: about 250–750 V at 50 Hz for 0.25–1 s. The DC defibrillator stores energy in a capacitor and releases it in one pulse:
answer.pre:
32 µF at 5000 V: E = ½ × 32 × 10⁻⁶ × 5000² = 400 J stored
with 10 Ω inside and 50 Ω chest: 50 / 60 × 400 = 333 J delivered

answer: DC replaced AC because it defibrillates with less muscle damage and fewer arrhythmias, its energy can be set and measured, and it can run from a battery. "AC-powered" today means only that the charger runs from mains.

Pulse energy and shock energy. A defibrillation shock of 200 J is about 200 ÷ 6.25 × 10⁻⁶ = 3.2 × 10⁷ times a pacing pulse: pacing excites a small patch and lets the beat spread, while defibrillation must depolarise most of the ventricle at once.

head: Hazard
Device
Control
rows: X-ray and threshold checks, lead replacement
sterile implantation, early removal of temporary wires
EMI from MRI, diathermy, strong magnets
gel pads, good contact, correct pad size

answer: Closing check: 6.25 µJ against 19.6 mJ and 333 J; ½ × 32 µF × 5000² = 400 J.

bank.q: Analyze why dry oxygen injures the airway and how humidifier or nebulizer settings correct this. Include hazards of over-humidification and infection.
outline: Dry gas damages cilia and mucosa
answer: Why dry gas injures the airway. Normally the nose warms and wets inspired air, so that below the carina it is at 37 °C and saturated (44 mg/L), the isothermic saturation boundary. Dry oxygen, or any gas given through a tube or tracheostomy, pushes that boundary deep into the lungs, and the lower airway gives up its own water and heat.

head: Stage
Effect
rows: collapse of lung units, infection, blocked tube

answer.pre:
dry oxygen, 10 L/min: 44 mg/L × 10 = 440 mg/min = 26.4 g/h
room air 25 °C, 50 % RH: 0.5 × 23 = 11.5 mg/L present
  deficit 44 − 11.5 = 32.5 mg/L → 325 mg/min = 19.5 g/h

answer: Water vapour versus droplets. A humidifier adds vapour, single water molecules that stay in the gas and reach every airway. A nebulizer adds droplets; droplets of 1–5 µm settle in the bronchi and alveoli, larger ones rain out in the tubing and throat, and droplets do not raise the humidity of the gas much. So humidity is corrected with a humidifier, and drugs are given with a nebulizer.

Nebulizer settings. A jet nebulizer is driven by 6–8 L/min, gives MMAD 1–5 µm and leaves about 1 mL unused in the cup. In a ventilator circuit it goes in the inspiratory limb, and an HME must be removed while it runs, because the HME traps the aerosol and its resistance rises.

head: Hazard
Cause
Prevention
rows: warm saturated gas cools in the tubing
heated-wire circuit, water traps below the patient
droplets plus vapour in small infants
temperature probe at the patient end with an alarm
sterile water, closed refill, circuit changes

answer: Effect on ventilator readings. A jet nebulizer adds its 6–8 L/min to the breath, so the delivered and exhaled volumes read high and the patient may not trigger; condensation in the expiratory filter raises resistance; water on a flow sensor makes the volume readings wrong; water sloshing in the tubing can trigger extra breaths.

bank.q: Evaluate the hazards of short-wave diathermy in a patient with a metallic implant or cardiac pacemaker. What precautions would you take?
outline: Radio-frequency current heats tissue and metal
answer: How short-wave diathermy heats. A 27.12 MHz field between capacitor plates, or from an induction coil, drives dielectric and resistive losses in the tissue. The wavelength, 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 27.12 × 10⁶ = 11.06 m, is far longer than the body, so the patient sits in the near field and anything conducting in that field also carries current.

answer.text: Hazard 1: a metallic implant. Metal conducts far better than tissue, so the field lines crowd onto it and the current density is highest at its ends and edges:

head: Effect
Result
rows: Current concentrates at the metal surface
deep burn next to the implant
The patient feels warmth only in the skin
the deep burn gives no warning
Metal jewellery, zips, hearing aids, metal couch

head: Effect
Result
rows: RF picked up by the lead and sensed as beats
output inhibited: asystole in a pacemaker-dependent patient
RF current induced in the lead
heating of the tissue at the lead tip, raising the pacing threshold

answer.pre:
short-wave: 200 W for 10 min → E = 200 × 600 = 120 kJ
ultrasound alternative: 1.5 W/cm² × 5 cm² = 7.5 W → 2250 J in 5 min

answer: Electrode placement and tuning. The plates are spaced evenly from the skin with dry towels, so the field is even; the cables are kept apart and away from the patient; the circuit is tuned to resonance with the patient so the power is delivered smoothly, and sweat is wiped away because water concentrates the field.

head: Step
Action
rows: ask about pacemakers, ICDs, cochlear implants, nerve stimulators, metal plates, joint replacements, IUDs, pregnancy; read the notes
remove jewellery, hearing aids and metal; use a wooden couch and chair
test hot and cold sensation over the area first
start low, ask about warmth every few minutes, use a timer, keep the call bell in the hand
keep the unit away from other patients' electronic devices; staff stand about 1–2 m away

answer: When diathermy is contraindicated. Any patient with a pacemaker, ICD or other implanted stimulator: do not use short-wave or microwave diathermy anywhere on the body, because the field and the leads extend widely. A metal implant in or near the treated area: do not treat that area with short-wave or microwave. Also pregnancy (abdomen and pelvis), loss of sensation, poor circulation, bleeding, malignancy and active infection in the field.

Evaluation. The precautions reduce but do not remove the risk, because the hazard comes from physics, not from operator error. Where a contraindication exists, choose another treatment: ultrasound away from the device, hot packs, exercise or TENS with the pacemaker team's agreement.

bank.q: Explain how an ablation catheter and its radio-frequency generator treat supraventricular tachycardia. Relate its safety principles to defibrillator protection.
outline: Protection of ECG amplifiers from high energy
answer: Supraventricular tachycardia. Most SVT is a re-entry circuit with a small critical part: a slow pathway near the AV node (AV nodal re-entry), an accessory pathway between atrium and ventricle (as in Wolff–Parkinson–White), or a single atrial focus. Destroying a few millimetres of that tissue cures it.

Focus mapping. Catheters passed from the femoral vein are placed at the high right atrium, the His bundle, the coronary sinus and the right ventricle. Their signals show the order of activation; programmed pacing starts the tachycardia so the earliest signal, the target, can be found. A 3D mapping system shows the activation as a colour map of the chamber.

head: Part
Design
Value
rows: steerable by pull wires, about 7 F (2.33 mm), with a thermocouple in the tip
large pad on the back or thigh
power, tip temperature, impedance and time limits

answer.text: Power at the tip (50 W into 100 Ω):
Why the heating stays at the tip. The same current crosses a small tip and a large pad:
answer.pre:
tip area ≈ π × 2.33 × 4 + π × 2.33² / 4 = 29.3 + 4.3 = 33.6 mm²
tip current density = 707 mA / 33.6 mm² = 21 mA/mm²
pad: 100 cm² = 10 000 mm², about 300 times larger, so about 1/300 of the density

answer: Controlled heating and lesion formation. Resistive heating is greatest in the thin tissue layer touching the tip; heat conducts outward and tissue above about 50 °C dies, making a lesion a few millimetres deep. The generator throttles power to hold the tip at 60–70 °C; above about 100 °C blood boils and forms a coagulum on the tip.

Impedance as a safety signal. A fall of 5–10 Ω during delivery shows the tissue is heating. A sudden rise shows coagulum on the tip, so the generator cuts out. Each burn is applied for 30–60 s and the circuit is retested; if the tachycardia can no longer be started, the ablation is done. Near the AV node, cryoablation may be used because its effect can be tested and reversed before it is permanent.

head: Idea
Ablation
Defibrillator protection
rows: power, temperature and time limits in the generator
series resistors limit current: 5000 V / 40 kΩ = 125 mA
dispersive pad spreads the return current
neon lamp shunts the shock, diodes clamp the rest
filters remove 500 kHz from the intracardiac and surface ECG
the network stops 5000 V reaching the amplifier
trace saturated for up to a few seconds

answer: The lab must also be ready to defibrillate, because pacing the circuit can start atrial or ventricular fibrillation; the ECG amplifiers in the recording system therefore need the same defibrillation protection.

Patient and operator safety. Patient: full pad contact, since a half-detached pad concentrates the current and burns the skin; watch for perforation and tamponade, AV block and clots; low leakage currents through the catheters, because a direct path to the heart makes microshock possible. Operator: lead aprons, thyroid shields and pulsed low-dose fluoroscopy against the X-ray dose.

glossary.def: A device that gives a small timed electrical pulse to the heart when natural conduction fails.
A device that delivers a large controlled shock to stop ventricular fibrillation.
A heart-lung machine circuit that pumps and oxygenates blood while the heart is stopped.
A machine that moves a breath into the lungs and lets it out.
A device that adds water vapour to dry medical gas.
A device that turns liquid into fine droplets for inhalation.
A device that delivers a measured drug dose to the airway.
Deep heating of tissue by radio-frequency current, microwaves or ultrasound.
Diathermy using radio-frequency current, commonly 27.12 MHz.
Diathermy using microwave energy, commonly 2.45 GHz.
Deep heating by high-frequency sound waves passed into tissue.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, used mainly for pain relief.
Neuromuscular electrical stimulation, used to make muscles contract.
Electrical muscle stimulation, a general term for current pulses that cause muscle contraction.
Functional electrical stimulation, NMES timed to help a useful movement.
A short interrupted current used to stimulate nerve and muscle.
A steady direct current used in some electrotherapy treatments.
A medium-frequency alternating current used for muscle strengthening.
Two crossed medium-frequency currents that produce a low difference frequency in tissue.
Breaking a kidney stone with focused shock waves.
Destruction of tissue by local freezing below about −40 °C.
A circuit that protects an ECG amplifier from a defibrillator shock.
A catheter that delivers radio-frequency energy to destroy an arrhythmia-causing patch of heart muscle.
The on-time of one electrical pulse.
Current multiplied by pulse width, Q = I × t, in coulombs.
